{
  "text": "## The Efficacy of Postoperative Prophylactic Antibiotics in Orthognathic Surgery: A Prospective Study in Le Fort I Osteotomy and Bilateral Intraoral Vertical Ramus Osteotomy\n\n## INTRODUCTION\nAntibiotics are used to treat and prevent postoperative infections. In 1960, it was reported that pathogens are present during surgery[1],[2] regardless of how aseptic the surgery might appear. Moreover, the correlation between prophylactic antibiotics and postoperative wound infections was demonstrated. Therefore, prophylactic antibiotics are now used in almost all surgical procedures. The most effective method of antibiotic prophylaxis is the preoperative administration of antibiotics because it can act at the time when the wound is potentially contaminated by bacteria.[2]\u207b[4] On the other hand, it was also reported that the use of antibiotics after 3 - 4 hours of a bacterial invasion is unsuitable.[5]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics are generally administered both preoperatively and postoperatively. Hence, the effects of the indiscriminate method and period of administration are unclear, considering the multiple factors that contribute to postoperative wound infections.[6]\u207b[8]\n\nThe use of antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial even in orthognathic surgery, which is a representative procedure for oral and maxillofacial surgery. There are reports show no increase in the incidence of infection without the administration of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics.[9],[10] On the other hand, there are reports to suggest the necessity of continuous antibiotic administration.[11] However, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without a specific medical history. Moreover, the number of factors associated with the development of postoperative wound infections decreases as the procedure becomes more generalized and its technique advances.\n\nThe aims of this clinical study were to evaluate the prevalence of postoperative wound infections with or without antibiotic prophylaxis after orthognathic surgery in young patients without any specific medical history, and to identify criteria for appropriate use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery.\n\n## PATIENTS AND METHODS\nFifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history, and who were to undergo orthognathic surgical procedures at the department of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the dental hospital of Yonsei University were enrolled in this study. A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon with the aid of trained nurses and residents under hypotensive general anesthesia. No bone grafts were performed. The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours. During surgery, maxillomandibular fixation was placed using steel wires, and drainage tubes were placed on both sides of the mandible. The drainage tubes were removed 2 days after surgery. The wires used for maxillomandibular fixation were removed and the sutures were taken out from the wounds 7 days after surgery. The patients received a non-steroid anti-inflammatory drug (Ketorolac trometamine 30 mg) intramuscularly immediately after surgery and every 6 hours until the next day. Compression bandages and ice packs were applied to the facial area until the second day after surgery.\n\nThe 56 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel: an experimental and control group. The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo. The control group also received 1.0 g of Cefpiramide 30 minutes before surgery as well as twice daily until 3 days after surgery. The patients were evaluated every day during the first 3 days and at the end of the 1st and 2nd week after surgery for any postoperative infections in reference to the criteria for defining a surgical site infection (SSI), recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).[12] Postoperative wound infection was defined by at least 1 of the following criteria:\n\nStatistical analysis was performed using a \u03c7\u00b2-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the College of Dentistry, Yonsei University (YUDC).\n\n## RESULTS\nThe mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84) with male-female ratio of 4 : 3. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 40 minutes. The mean (SD) age of the control group was 24.3 years (6.33) with male-female ratio of 1 : 1. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 55 minutes.\n\nThere were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group, observed 2 weeks after surgery (Table 1). One patient in the experimental group was diagnosed with an infection by facial swelling, redness and sinus haziness in the waters' view, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with a postoperative infection by swelling and redness, and pain on the mandibular area. Therefore, the wounds were opened by a surgeon and the patients were treated with antibiotics. However, only 1 patient in the control group developed wound dehiscence only without any drainage, fever, or swelling in the maxillary area. According to the \u03c7\u00b2-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).\n\n[Table 1: Results according to the Postoperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis \u2014 image only, no cells; see tables]\n\n## DISCUSSION\nThe method of antibiotic prophylaxis is determined by an evaluation of the patient, procedure, and surgical wound. The preoperative and immediate postoperative administration of antibiotics is a method generally used for antibiotic prophylaxis in almost all surgical procedures. However, antibiotics are continuously used postoperatively in most procedures because it is difficult to assess the factors associated with postoperative wound infections or appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis method.\n\nOn the other hand, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without an underlying illness or comorbidity. Moreover, the number of factors affecting the development of postoperative wound infections decreases with the improvement of the surgical instruments, materials, techniques, and more generalized procedure.\n\nPeterson[13] suggested that the prophylactic antibiotic administration for postoperative wound infections in oral and maxillofacial surgery should be performed if there is a strong probability of infection, and appropriate antibiotics must be given in high-dose but for only a short period of time. Orthognathic surgeries are classified as clean contaminated procedures with postoperative wound infection of 10% to 15%, and Peterson[13] reported that an incidence of an anticipated infection in oral clean contaminated surgery could be reduced by using prophylactic antibiotics. Zijderveld et al.[14] suggested that the incidence of postoperative infections (52.6%) increased without the administration of prophylactic antibiotics. Martis and Karabouta[9] suggested that the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery is unnecessary, and Lindeboom et al.[15] also suggested that the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics (clindamycin) is unnecessary in orthognathic surgery (SSRO). Furthermore, Fridrich et al.[16] and Baqain et al.[17] suggested that the long-term use of antibiotics does not decrease the frequency of postoperative infections. However, wide range of patient's age, small group size, and various osteomies may cause difficulties when precisely evaluating the efficacy of prophylactic antibiotics.\n\nTherefore, this study was undertaken to examine the prevalence of postoperative wound infections in young patients after orthognathic surgery (Le Fort I osteotomy and bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy) with or without the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics. Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of \u03b1= 0.05 and a test power \u03b2= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.[17] In this study, wound infections were observed in both groups, however, the number was small. This was attributed to the followings: the patients were young without a specific medical history, patients had no preoperative wound infections, no bone graft had been performed during surgery, the surgical procedures such as IVRO were less traumatic with a short duration, the tissue trauma during surgery was minimal due to the systematization of orthognathic surgery and the improvement of techniques, and wound control such as postoperative blood or exudate was properly performed.\n\nThe types of antibiotics used are important factors to consider for prophylactic antibiotic treatment. Penicillin is the representative antibiotic used as a prophylaxis during intraoral surgery and for the primary treatment of dental infections. Spaey et al[18] suggested the use of amoxicillin-clavulanate along with drain usage during SSRO in a study of antibiotic administration. In this study, third-generation cephalosporin antibiotics were administered before surgery, which is believed to be a possible prophylactic antibiotic that may be used in orthognathic surgery because most bacteria cultured during a dental infection are susceptible to third-generation cephalosporin.[19] There has been an increase in infections due to anaerobic and Gram-negative organisms,[20] and most wound infections after orthognathic surgery are caused by Gram negative bacteria.[21]\n\nIf a post-operative wound infection occurs despite the effective prophylactic antibiotic administration before surgery, it could be concluded that the bacteria in the infected wound are not sensitive to the prophylactic antibiotics administered, and in such cases, an appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be determined by a culture test of the bacteria found in the infected region.[21],[22]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics reduce the risk of postoperative wound infections, which leads to a lower number of hospitalization days, reduced cost, and improved social life. However, the long-term use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics may lead to several problems, such as various allergic reactions, increased cost, changes in resident bacterial colony in vivo, or appearance of resistant bacteria.[7],[23]\n\nMore studies with much larger numbers of patients are needed on the administration of prophylactic antibiotics during orthognathic surgery and other oral and maxillofacial procedures. In addition, further research on properly appropriated use of antibiotic prophylaxis is warranted in order to minimize the use of prophylactic antibiotics and their adverse effects and problems. In the present study, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who did not. Therefore, prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections.\n\n## References\n\n# References\n\n1. headline.statement: Every number this five-page trial prints reconciles with the statistics beside it -- the sole p-value reproduces exactly from the counts in Table 1, all four count rows sum, and both age mean/SD pairs are reconstructible -- but the paper's conclusion that prolonged prophylaxis "may not be necessary" is an acceptance of the null stated with no confidence interval, from a trial sized to detect only a 30-percentage-point difference in infection rate.
headline.evidence: Table 1: "Postoperative infection (n) 3 | 2" in arms of "(n=28)" and "(n=28)"; Results: "According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections ... (p = 0.639)." Recomputed from the printed 2x2 [[3,25],[2,26]]: Pearson χ²(1) = 0.2196, p = 0.639339 -- matching the printed 0.639 to three decimals. Counts: 16+12 = 28, 14+14 = 28, 28+28 = 56, 3+2 = 5, all exact. Ages 23.9 ± 5.84 and 24.3 ± 6.33 at n = 28 both admit valid integer (sum, sum-of-squares) solutions. Design, from the Discussion: "A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%".
headline.plain: This small trial's numbers all add up: the one statistical test it reports can be recalculated exactly from the patient counts printed in its table, and nothing in the paper contradicts anything else. What the paper cannot support is how confidently it reads its own result -- it found 3 infections in one group and 2 in the other, which tells you almost nothing, and it never says how big a real difference could still be hiding behind that.

findings.title: Null conclusion drawn with no confidence interval, from a design sized only for a 30-percentage-point difference
findings.location: Abstract (Results and Conclusion); Results, final paragraph; Discussion, sample-size paragraph
findings.reported: "Conclusion: Prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections." The supporting evidence is p = 0.639 alone. The Discussion states the design: "The samples were selected at a significance level of α=0.05 and a test power β=0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%". No confidence interval, effect size, or risk difference is reported anywhere in the paper.
findings.computed: recalc_chi_squared on the printed 2x2 [[3,25],[2,26]] returns a Fisher odds ratio of 1.56 -- the point estimate favours MORE infection in the arm that received fewer antibiotics, the opposite direction from the conclusion's framing, though on 3 versus 2 events it is indistinguishable from no difference (Fisher p = 1.0). The trial's own stated target was a 5% versus 35% infection rate; the observed contrast is 3/28 versus 2/28, a difference of one patient. No registered tool in this kit derives a confidence interval from a 2x2 count table, so the largest difference these data still permit could not be quantified -- that gap is recorded rather than estimated.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The design parameters (α = 0.05, 5% smaller rate, 30% difference, 28 per group) and the event counts are all quoted as printed. The odds ratio of 1.56 is tool output, not hand arithmetic. The direction of the point estimate is noted, not interpreted as evidence of harm.

consequence.explanation: The paper's single recommendation -- that prolonged postoperative prophylaxis may be unnecessary -- is argued from a non-significant p-value alone, with nothing stating how large a clinically meaningful difference in infection rate the trial could still have missed.

findings.plain: The trial was built to spot a very large difference: roughly 5 out of 100 patients getting infected in one group versus 35 out of 100 in the other. What it actually saw was 3 infections against 2. With numbers that small, a difference that would matter to a real patient could easily be present and go undetected -- and the paper never says what range of differences its data can rule out. So "we found no difference" is not the same as "there is no difference", and the recommendation to stop antibiotics earlier rests on the weaker of those two. Note this is a limitation of what the study can conclude, not a sign that any number in it is wrong; the authors are unusually open about their design assumptions, which is what makes this visible at all.

findings.title: Chi-squared applied where expected cell counts are 2.5, half the conventional minimum
findings.location: Patients and Methods, statistical analysis sentence; Results, final paragraph; against Table 1 infection row
findings.reported: "Statistical analysis was performed using a χ²-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA)." The test is applied to 3 infections of 28 versus 2 of 28, and reported as p = 0.639. No exact test is mentioned.
findings.computed: recalc_chi_squared returns expected counts of 2.5 in both infection cells -- half the conventional minimum of 5 for the chi-squared approximation. The reported p = 0.639 is reproduced exactly by the uncorrected Pearson statistic (χ²(1) = 0.2196, p = 0.639339), which identifies the convention used. The two alternatives appropriate to these counts both give p = 1.0: Yates-corrected χ² = 0.0000, and Fisher's exact p = 1.0.
findings.assumptions: The 5-per-cell minimum for the chi-squared approximation is Cochran's conventional rule (Cochran 1954), an external norm this paper never claims to follow. Uncorrected 2x2 chi-squared on small counts was routine in clinical reporting in 2008-2009, when this was submitted and published.

consequence.explanation: The stated finding of no difference stands under every convention -- Pearson p = 0.639, Yates p = 1.0 and Fisher's exact p = 1.0 are all non-significant -- so the test choice makes the reported p optimistically precise rather than wrong in direction.

findings.plain: The statistical test the authors used is an approximation that needs a reasonable number of expected events in each cell of the table; here it expects only 2.5, about half what the rule of thumb asks for. A different test designed for small counts is the standard choice in that situation. It changes nothing about the answer -- every version of the test says the same thing, that no difference was detected -- but it means the specific number 0.639 should not be read as precise.

The chi-squared value and its degrees of freedom appear nowhere in the paper.

consequence.explanation: The paper's sole confirmatory claim would have been unverifiable by any reader had Table 1 not independently printed the four cell counts the test was computed from.

findings.plain: When researchers report a statistical test, they normally print the test's own value alongside the p-value, so a reader can check that the two agree. This paper prints only the p-value. It happens to be correct -- the counts in the table let us recompute it and it matches exactly -- but that was luck of layout rather than design: if the table had shown percentages instead of patient counts, the paper's one and only statistical claim could not have been checked by anyone.

findings.plain: Deciding whether a surgical wound is infected involves judgement calls about swelling, redness and pain. In this trial the surgeon who performed every operation also knew which patients had been given the extra antibiotics, and no one independent was brought in to make that call. That does not mean the counts are wrong, and the paper is upfront that no dummy treatment was used -- but a reader who assumes a randomised trial means an impartial assessment should know that this one did not have one.

input.report_markdown:
This is a small single-centre trial from Yonsei University asking whether prophylactic antibiotics need to be continued after orthognathic surgery. Fifty-six young patients undergoing Le Fort I osteotomy with bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy, all operated on by the same surgeon, were randomised by Excel-generated codes to receive a single 1.0 g preoperative dose of cefpiramide alone, or the same dose plus twice-daily cefpiramide to the third postoperative day. Surgical site infections were assessed at two weeks against CDC criteria. Three infections occurred in the experimental arm and two in the control arm, and the authors conclude that prolonged prophylaxis may not be necessary.

## What the checks bought

The arithmetic here is clean, and the cleanliness is worth stating precisely rather than in the aggregate. The paper's single inferential result reproduces exactly from the counts it prints: the 2x2 of 3/28 against 2/28 gives Pearson chi-squared of 0.2196 on one degree of freedom and p = 0.639339, against the printed p = 0.639. Every count reconciles with exact tolerance -- the sex counts against each arm (16 + 12 = 28, 14 + 14 = 28), the arms against the stated total (28 + 28 = 56), and the per-arm infections against the five patients narrated individually in the Results (3 + 2 = 5). Both age mean/SD pairs are reconstructible from integer ages at n = 28: valid sum and sum-of-squares combinations exist for 23.9 ± 5.84 and for 24.3 ± 6.33. That is what a carefully prepared paper looks like, and on a paper this short it is close to everything there was to check.

One qualification a reader is owed: the age means were not cleared by every available check. GRIM has no resolution at n = 28 with one decimal place, so it could not have caught anything there and correctly returned no verdict. GRIMMER, which can discriminate at these values, passed both.

## Where the trouble is, and where it is not

Nothing in this paper contradicts anything else in it. The open questions are all about what the result can be made to support.

The central one is that a conclusion of "no difference" is drawn from an event count of three against two. The paper is more forthcoming than most about how it was sized -- it states plainly that it targeted a contrast between a 5% and a 35% infection rate -- and that candour is what makes the problem legible. A trial built for a 30-percentage-point gap has essentially no purchase on the differences that would actually change clinical practice, and the paper reports no interval, no risk difference and no effect size that would tell a reader which differences remain live. The point estimate recoverable from the counts is an odds ratio of 1.56, pointing weakly toward more infection in the arm that received fewer antibiotics -- the opposite of the conclusion's direction, though on five events in total that is noise rather than signal. It cannot be given an interval here because no tool in this kit derives one from a 2x2 table, and that limitation is ours to own.

The test choice compounds this rather than causing it. Expected counts of 2.5 per infection cell are half what the chi-squared approximation conventionally wants, and the exact alternatives appropriate at these counts both return p = 1.0. The conclusion is unaffected in direction under every convention, so this makes the figure 0.639 falsely precise rather than wrong -- and uncorrected chi-squared on small 2x2 tables was ordinary practice in 2008. It is also worth noting that the paper reports neither the chi-squared statistic nor its degrees of freedom, so its one confirmatory claim was recoverable only because Table 1 happens to print patient counts rather than percentages.

Two design points belong beside these. The trial was randomised but not masked -- the paper says so directly, which is to its credit -- and two of the four CDC criteria it adopts are assessor-judged, with the assessment made by the surgeon who performed every operation and knew each allocation. And the study motivates itself by criticising earlier work for a "wide range of patient's age", while printing no age range of its own; its dispersion figures sit awkwardly with the phrase "in their 20s", though a lopsided age distribution would reconcile both without any reporting error, and the arithmetic of those figures checks out. I have graded that last point as unresolved rather than as a defect, because the paper is simply silent on the question and the innocent reading is at least as natural as the alternative.

A note on one thing I did not do. The sweep flagged both age standard deviations as exceeding what an age band of 20 to 29 permits. That band is a translation of prose, not a range the paper prints, and a bound the reviewer supplies can invert this kind of check rather than merely weaken it. It has been capped accordingly and is reported as an open question about missing information, not as an anomaly in the numbers.

The reported statistics in this paper verify against each other. What warrants caution is not the arithmetic but the strength of the inference drawn from five events.
